title: Rate Limiting, Resilience & Reliability
summary: Every system has a breaking point. These patterns decide whether a spike or a slow dependency becomes a graceful slowdown or a full outage.

blocks.markdown:
Resilience patterns keep demand below your limits and contain failures before they spread.

- **Rate limiting** bounds the input so a spike can't crash you.
- **Timeouts + circuit breakers** bound how long and how often you wait on a dependency.
- **Bulkheads** partition resources so one bad dependency can't sink everything.
- **Retries + idempotency** recover from transient blips without duplicates.
- **Load shedding + degradation** sacrifice the periphery to keep the core alive.

blocks.subTitle: Which tool for which problem
blocks.markdown:
Match the failure mode to the pattern.

| Situation | Reach for |
|---|---|
| Cap a caller's rate, allow bursts | Token bucket |
| Downstream is failing or slow | Breaker + timeout |
| A transient blip (503, reset) | Retry + backoff + jitter |
| One dep must not sink the app | Bulkhead |
| Past capacity, protect core | Shed load + degrade |

blocks.subTitle: Why systems collapse
blocks.markdown:
Systems don't degrade gracefully on their own — they fall off a cliff.

- Past capacity, queues build, each request waits longer, threads stay busy longer, so the queue grows *faster*. Throughput drops toward zero — **congestion collapse**.
- When one service slows, callers' threads pile up waiting; the slowness propagates outward and takes down healthy services — a **cascading failure**.
- The network is unreliable: packets drop, connections reset. Many failures are transient, which is why retries matter — but they must be disciplined.

blocks.subTitle: Token bucket
blocks.markdown:
The default rate limiter: a bucket of up to **B** tokens, refilled at **r** per second. Each request takes a token; an empty bucket means rejected.

![Token bucket algorithm](assets/rate-limiting-resilience/token-bucket.svg)

- Quiet periods let tokens accumulate, so a **burst of up to B** is served instantly.
- Long-run rate can't exceed **r** — that's how fast tokens refill.
- Cheap and lazy: store `tokens` and `last_refill`, compute the refill on each request. No timer needed.
- Most APIs (Stripe, AWS) use it because real traffic is bursty.

blocks.subTitle: The other limiter algorithms
blocks.markdown:
They differ in how they treat bursts and memory.

- **Leaky bucket** — requests queue and drain at a constant rate; output is perfectly smooth, no bursts. Best for a fragile backend, but adds latency.
- **Fixed window** — count per clock window, reset on rollover. Dead simple, but allows a **2x burst** at the window edge.
- **Sliding window log** — store a timestamp per request; exact but memory grows with volume.
- **Sliding window counter** — blend current and previous window counts. Cheap, smooth, what most production limiters use.

blocks.subTitle: Distributed rate limiting
blocks.markdown:
With many servers, per-server limits silently multiply by the server count.

- 10 servers each allowing 100/min lets a caller do **1000/min**. To enforce a global cap, all servers share one counter — almost always in **Redis** ([caching](caching)).
- The check-and-increment must be **atomic** (Lua script or `INCR`), or two servers race, both read 99, both allow.
- Cost: a Redis round-trip per request (~1 ms) and a new dependency.
- To cut load, give each server a local slice of the budget and reconcile periodically — less precise, far fewer Redis calls.

blocks.subTitle: Timeouts & retries
blocks.markdown:
A timeout caps how long you wait — the most important resilience setting, because an untimed call hangs forever and holds a thread.

```python
attempt = 0
while attempt < MAX_RETRIES:
    r = call()
    if r.ok: return r
    if not is_retryable(r): raise   # e.g. 400, 404
    cap = min(MAX_BACKOFF, BASE * 2 ** attempt)
    sleep(random_uniform(0, cap))   # full jitter
    attempt += 1
```

- **Exponential backoff** gives a struggling service room to recover.
- **Jitter** spreads synchronized retries so they don't re-overload in waves.
- Cap attempts and bound retries to a small fraction of traffic (a retry budget).

blocks.subTitle: Circuit breaker
blocks.markdown:
A breaker wraps a dependency and stops calling it once it's clearly broken — fail fast instead of piling up doomed calls.

![Circuit breaker state machine](assets/rate-limiting-resilience/circuit-breaker.svg)

- **Closed** — calls pass through; count failures. Cross a threshold (e.g. >50% of last 20) and trip to Open.
- **Open** — fail immediately for a cooldown (e.g. 30 s), freeing threads and giving the dependency room to recover.
- **Half-open** — after cooldown, let a few probes through; succeed → Closed, fail → Open.
- Pair with a **fallback**, or fail-fast just means error-fast.

blocks.subTitle: Bulkheads & idempotency
blocks.markdown:
A bulkhead gives each dependency its own pool so one saturated dependency can't starve the others.

![Bulkhead isolation](assets/rate-limiting-resilience/bulkhead.svg)

- If pool B hangs, calls to A and C have their own threads and keep working — only that feature degrades.
- **Idempotency** makes retries safe: doing the operation twice has the same effect as once.
- The technique is an **idempotency key** — the client sends a unique key; the server stores and *replays* the result instead of re-executing. Stripe does this for payments.

blocks.subTitle: Picking a limiter
blocks.markdown:
All cap a rate — they trade bursts against memory and accuracy.

| Algorithm | Bursts | Memory |
|---|---|---|
| Token bucket | Up to B | O(1) |
| Leaky bucket | None | O(1)+queue |
| Fixed window | 2x at edge | O(1) |
| Sliding counter | Slight | O(1) |

Default to **token bucket**; leaky bucket only when a fragile backend needs smooth input; sliding window counter for very high volume.

blocks.subTitle: The constant tensions
blocks.markdown:
Every choice here trades one good thing against another.

- **Throughput vs. protection** — tight limits reject legitimate traffic; loose limits risk overload.
- **Latency vs. accuracy** — a global Redis counter is exact but adds a round-trip; local buckets are fast but approximate.
- **Availability vs. correctness** — retries raise success but, without idempotency, risk duplicates.
- **Isolation vs. efficiency** — dedicated pools contain failure but leave capacity idle.

blocks.subTitle: Real systems & signals
blocks.markdown:
These patterns are battle-tested infrastructure, not theory.

- **Stripe** — an `Idempotency-Key` header; it stores the first response and replays it on retry, so a blip can't double-charge.
- **AWS** — SDKs use full jitter by default after synchronized retries caused thundering herds.
- **Netflix Hystrix** — wrapped every call in a breaker + timeout + bulkhead + fallback. Now pushed into proxies like **Envoy** ([load-balancing-proxies](load-balancing-proxies)).
- **Watch**: 429 rate, breaker trips, retry ratio (>10% = trouble), timeout rate, p99/p999 latency.

The mistakes that turn a recoverable slowdown into an outage:

- **Per-server limits add up.** Without a shared store, your "global" limit is multiplied by the server count.
- **Naive retries.** No backoff, jitter, or budget turns a blip into a self-inflicted DDoS.
- **A timeout is the foundation, not a nice-to-have.** Most cascade outages trace to a missing one.
- **An open breaker only stops the bleeding.** Without a fallback, users just get errors fast.
- **Idempotency is not a unique constraint.** True idempotency *replays the original result* for a repeated key.
